extracted.intended_audience: litigators and regulatory counsel handling Hatch-Waxman/Orange Book disputes; patent attorneys for branded and generic pharmaceutical companies; judges and law clerks in pharmaceutical patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and interpretive criteria for whether a patent may be listed in the FDA Orange Book (and for a generic applicant’s delisting counterclaim) under the FDCA, the Orange Book Transparency Act (OBTA), and related Hatch‑Waxman provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory listing requirement (21 U.S.C. § 355(b)(1)(A)(viii))
rubrics_metrics.description: An NDA holder must submit “the patent number and expiration date of each patent for which a claim of patent infringement could reasonably be asserted if a person not licensed by the owner engaged in the manufacture, use, or sale of the drug,” and the listed patent must (I) “claim the drug for which the applicant submitted the application and is a drug substance (active ingredient) patent or a drug product (formulation or composition) patent” or (II) claim a method of using such drug.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OBTA (2021) amended the provision and added explicit language that certain other patent information “shall not be submitted,” thereby setting both a floor and a ceiling for listable patents; Congress intended the amended language to codify FDA regulations (21 C.F.R. § 314.53(b)(1)). Treat the statutory text as imposing two distinct requirements: (a) a patent be one for which a claim of infringement could reasonably be asserted, and (b) it must additionally be a patent that actually ‘claims the drug’ (as further defined elsewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'claims' (35 U.S.C. § 112(b) / patent law)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent 'claims' subject matter by the claim language that 'particularly point[s] out and distinctly claim[s] the subject matter which the inventor ... regards as the invention' (35 U.S.C. § 112(b)); claims and the specification read together define the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For listing purposes, 'claims' should be interpreted according to patent-law claim construction principles: the court must look to what the patent particularly points out and distinctly claims, not simply whether a product would infringe the claim. Do not conflate the statutory word 'claims' with the separate concept of infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 'claims' and 'infringement' in listing analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The listing provision requires both that (1) 'a claim of patent infringement could reasonably be asserted' and (2) that the patent 'claims the drug.' These are distinct statutory predicates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An interpretation equating 'claims' with 'reads on' or 'infringes' creates redundancy and is disfavored. Courts should give effect to both statutory requirements; a patent may be infringed by a product without the patent 'claiming the drug' as that phrase is statutorily used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent must claim at least the active ingredient to 'claim the drug'
rubrics_metrics.description: To 'claim the drug for which the applicant submitted the application,' a patent must claim at least the active ingredient (the drug substance) that made the product approvable as a drug.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FDCA and case law treat the active ingredient as central to drug approval (labels, ANDA requirements, and FDA review focus on active ingredient). Accordingly, patents that only claim device components (e.g., dose counters, canister parts) do not 'claim the drug' for listing purposes unless they actually claim the active ingredient or a drug product/formulation that includes it.

rubrics_metrics.name: OBTA's 'drug-substance/drug-product' limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The OBTA added that a patent that 'claims the drug for which the applicant submitted the application' must be 'a drug substance (active ingredient) patent or a drug product (formulation or composition) patent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This legislative change narrows listable patents to typical drug-substance or drug-product patents (or method-of-use patents). Patents that fall outside those categories are not to be submitted per the OBTA language ('shall not be submitted'). The court noted this language but did not have to reach every consequence of it in the decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: FDA's ministerial role on Orange Book accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The FDA historically considers its role in Orange Book listing to be ministerial and does not substantively review patent information for accuracy or relevance to an NDA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the FDA does not police accuracy, parties must rely on statutory mechanisms (e.g., paragraph IV litigation and the counterclaim in § 355(j)(5)(C)(ii)(I)) or courts to challenge inaccurate listings; courts have upheld the FDA's non-review position as reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph I/II/III/IV certifications and timing consequences (21 U.S.C. § 355(j)(2)(A)(vii) and § 355(j)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: A generic ANDA applicant must make one of four certifications regarding listed patents: paragraph I (no patent information filed), paragraph II (patent expired), paragraph III (patent will expire on a stated date), or paragraph IV (patent is invalid or will not be infringed). Paragraph I/II can permit immediate approval; paragraph III defers approval until patent expiry; paragraph IV triggers a 45‑day window for the patent owner to sue, and if suit is filed the approval is stayed for thirty months (subject to exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These certification consequences create incentives to list or delist patents. The 30‑month stay is a powerful practical effect of listing and is central to the delisting counterclaim context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delisting counterclaim scope (§ 355(j)(5)(C)(ii)(I))
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patent owner sues after receiving a paragraph IV notice, the applicant may assert a counterclaim seeking an order requiring the holder to 'correct or delete' the patent information submitted on the ground that the patent does not claim (aa) the drug for which the application was approved or (bb) an approved method of using the drug.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The counterclaim is a limited but potent remedy because a successful delisting can convert a paragraph IV to a paragraph I (or otherwise eliminate the 30‑month stay). A generic applicant cannot bring a delisting action outside this counterclaim context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination-product treatment does not convert device subparts into 'the drug'
rubrics_metrics.description: Approval of a combination product via an NDA (because the product's primary mode of action is that of a drug) does not make every component of the combination product a 'drug.' Device components retain their identity as device parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For listing, the patent must claim the part that made the product approvable as a drug (i.e., the active ingredient/ drug-substance). Use the SMDA framework: determine primary mode of action and treat constituent parts according to their identities; inclusion in an NDA does not transform device patents into drug patents for listing purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction applies to listing inquiry (but formal Markman not always required)
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining what a patent 'claims' for listing/delisting, courts apply patent claim construction principles (Markman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A full Markman hearing is not required in every case; courts may adopt reasonable claim constructions on the pleadings for purposes of deciding a delisting question, citing precedent (e.g., Jazz Pharms., Aatrix). Still, the statutory requirement that claims 'particularly point out and distinctly claim' remains controlling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must particularly point out the specific approved active ingredient (not generic/overbroad 'active drug')
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that merely requires the presence of 'an active drug' (i.e., any active ingredient) is too broad to 'particularly point out and distinctly claim' the specific drug approved in an NDA (which identifies a specific active ingredient and often concentration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For listing, courts expect claims to identify the specific active ingredient (and, where relevant, the formulation parameters that were the basis for approval). Broad, unspecified active‑ingredient language does not satisfy the statutory requirement to 'claim the drug for which the applicant submitted the application.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Drug v. device functional/structural distinction (what makes something a 'drug')
rubrics_metrics.description: A drug is distinguished from a device in that a drug 'furnishes pharmacological activity' and achieves its primary intended purpose through chemical action or metabolization; devices are characterized more by their purely mechanical nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the chemical-action/metabolization touchstone (Bacto‑Unidisk; Genus Med.; Ipsen) to decide whether a claimed invention is a drug-substance/product or a device; only patents to the drug-substance/product side will generally be listable as 'claiming the drug.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory interpretation principles applied to the listing/delisting provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: In construing the listing and delisting provisions courts begin with the statutory language and interpret it in its specific and broader statutory context, giving effect where possible to every word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid readings that render statutory subparagraphs redundant; interpret 'for which the applicant submitted the application' and 'for which the application was approved' in light of the overall FDA/ANDA/Hatch‑Waxman scheme and legislative history (Caraco, Sandoz, etc.). Context and scheme determine meaning.
